newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian shares boosted by Dow, semiconductor report.
newsitem.headline: Asian shares boosted by Dow, semiconductor report.

text.p: Asian stocks were lifted on Tuesday by the U.S. markets' strong performance and news of increased semiconductor orders that led investors to snap up high-technology shares.
In Japan the key Nikkei 225 stood at 21,206.43, up 141.35 points, or 0.67 percent.
"Major issues headed by chip makers were well sought after," said Kenzo Doi, Kokusai Securities strategist.
Overnight in New York, the Dow leaped 36 points to about 6,256, closing higher for the fourth consecutive session.

The U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association's announcement that its book-to-bill ratio, which measures the value of orders against shipments, rose to 1.10 in October from a revised 0.98 in September, bolstered the market further.
"High-tech shares were bought, activating the market but momentum was not that strong and investors were not chasing share prices to new highs," one broker said.
Market sentiment was also helped by Japan's Economic Planning Agency, which reported the economy was moving gradually forward, brokers said.
The semiconductor report also helped Korean shares, which recorded their highest rise so far this year.
The composite stock index ended 3.15 percent, or 23.01 points, higher at a provisional 752.54.
"Today's rise is the highest this year. It showed sentiment has firmed," said Choo Hee-yup of Dongwon Securities.
Brokers said lingering market talk on government steps to boost investment was the main factor affecting the market.

The rumoured steps include cutting a tax on securities transactions, providing tax incentives to long-term stockholders and increasing the return on customer deposits at brokerage houses, brokers said. The government declined to comment.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index squeaked to a record close after a mixed session which was buoyed by late European interest and some laggard chasing, traders said.
The Hang Seng index closed 34.45 points higher at 12,806.31. The previous record close was on November 6 at 12,775.47.
Malaysian blue-chip stocks ended sharply higher as local and foreign institutional investors moved into the Kuala Lumpur bourse, dealers said.

"Foreign buyers may be in today, but EPF (Employees Provident Fund) and PNB (Permodalan Nasional Bhd) have both been buying," said an institutional dealer at a local securities brokerage company. EPF is the Malaysian state-run pension fund, while PNB is a savings fund for ethnic Malays.
The Composite Index was up 9.61 points to 1189.21, while the all-share EMAS index closed up 1.51 to 339.36.
Singapore shares were firm in late trading but a breakdown in the central computer of the Stock Exchange of Singapore hampered trading, dealers said.
The Straits Times Industrial index was up 10.94 points to 2,128.17 in late trade.
Australian shares slid after resource leaders ran into selling from offshore investors.
The All Ordinaries index fell 14.6 points to 2,343.5. News Corp posted an 8.1 percent drop in net profit for the three months to September 30.
Jakarta shares ended lower on follow-through profit-taking in secondaries and some heavyweights, brokers said.
The Jakarta Composite Index fell 4.08 points, or 0.68 percent, to close at 597.05 points after touching an intra-day low of 596.08 points.
At 1115 GMT the dollar was trading at 111.36/11.41 yen and 1.4945 marks.
Oil futures were lower on technical factors. SIMEX December crude traded at $22.95 per barrel, down six cents from its close on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) on Monday.
Gold bullion ended at US$381.60/382.10 an ounce against New York's US$381.50/381.90 close on Monday.
